Pour mon deuxième portrait des éducatric: For my second portrait of childcare educators and providers, I chose to introduce you to Lorena, a woman who decided to transform her career path to help children with disabilities.
En tant que mère de trois enfants présen: As the mother of three children on the autism spectrum, she not only found resources to improve their lives – a difficult mission, especially in the face of a serious shortage of solutions – but she also went further: Lorena decided to welcome children rejected by some facilities into her group at the daycare where she works.
Pendant notre conversation, j’ai remarqu: During our conversation, I noticed that Lorena often spoke of her “luck.” Reading the news, it’s easy to see why: most parents of neurodivergent children can’t find resources.
Si j’ai choisi cette histoire, c’est jus: I chose this story precisely because I believe that giving your children the support they are entitled to shouldn’t be a matter of luck. In my view, it’s thanks to people like Lorena that we may one day no longer have to rely on “luck.”
Ce nouveau portrait des éducatrices et g: This latest portrait of Quebec’s childcare educators and providers tells the story of Lorena, an immigrant woman and mother of three children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. She changed careers to care for children with disabilities, a field where the lack of support in the province is glaring.
Si vous ne connaissez pas Lorena et que: If you don’t know Lorena and you pass her on the street or on a bus, you’ll probably guess that she works with children. She has a very particular way of letting people know: she wears a pink hoodie that reads “Every child is unique,” with a heart in the middle.
« C’est une phrase que j’ai vue sur le m: “It’s a phrase I saw on the wall of my son’s classroom and I love it. I use it on different T-shirts and sweaters because I’m a spokesperson for inclusion. I also use it in the corner of my classroom, where I put up the activities my students do,” she says, smiling, with a joy and energy you can hear in her voice.
Lorena Morales est éducatrice en garderi: Lorena Morales is a daycare educator. In her classroom, she welcomes students with various types of learning difficulties, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD). According to data reported by the <l1>Observatoire des tout-petits</l1> (OTP) in 2022, the shortage of human resources led to a 20% reduction in the time children with disabilities spend in daycares.
Travailler dans un domaine aussi névralg: Working in such a critical field makes a big difference, she believes. “I ask [parents] a lot of questions because I know it’s essential to have a good relationship with the family.” She knows this all too well: she is the mother of three children diagnosed with ASD and had to learn to get familiar with the professionals responsible for caring for them. That’s how she learned the importance of empathy in her profession.
Au Venezuela, son pays d’origine, Lorena: In Venezuela, her home country, Lorena and her husband, Arturo, had good jobs and were moving forward in their careers. In 2015, a job offer for Arturo took them to London as expatriates. In 2017, Arturo was offered a new position in Montréal. The couple by then had three children: Adrián, born in Venezuela, and the twins Matias and Isabel, born in England.
Au Canada, les choses se présentent bien: In Canada, things were looking good. Lorena and her family settled in Brossard in 2018. Language was a challenge for them at first, but they loved the life they were building there. And then, one day, Lorena received a call from the daycare that would change their lives.
Lorena Morales avec ses trois enfants. P: Lorena Morales with her three children. Photo: Edouard Desroches
<strong>‍</strong>\n« Ils m’ont toujours: ‍ “They always told me Matías was different, but I never thought there was anything to worry about. Until they called me and talked about things I saw him do all the time: opening and closing drawers, staring at wheels, banging on the window. They asked me if anything worried me and pointed out, very kindly, that the things he was doing weren’t ‘normal’ for his age,” says Lorena.
« Au début, je pensais que l’éducatrice: “At first, I thought the educator was wrong, but I started watching Matías and reading up. And I realized something was going on.” She turned to her local community health centre (CLSC), which, after 10 months of assessments, forms and countless questions, gave her an official diagnosis: Matías is autistic. “Some parents wait three years, sometimes more, to get that confirmation,” Lorena points out. She then had her eldest son, Adrián, and Matías’s twin sister, Isabel, assessed.
Pour Adrián, le résultat est le même que: For Adrián, the result was the same as for his brother. “I wasn’t surprised by the diagnosis, because I had already prepared myself.” Isabel, however, who also has ASD, prompted a different reaction. “I had a harder time accepting that diagnosis,” she remembers.
Après le choc, tout devient beaucoup plu: After the shock, everything became much clearer: “I decided to get on that bus with everything I had and in my own way!” That’s how Lorena’s great adventure began.
La maman décide alors de suivre une form: The mother then decided to pursue training in education, a field that had always appealed to her. Her children’s diagnoses made her want to learn everything she could so she could help them have a better life. “When I saw special education on the list of subjects, I thought: ‘With everything I’ve learned here, I’m going to get full marks!’” She took an accelerated program and, within a year and a half, earned a diploma in early childhood education.
Pour son stage, elle pense immédiatement: For her internship, she immediately thought of the daycare her children had attended, she explains. “Because I’m immensely grateful to them.”
En 2023, Lorena est recrutée par cet éta: In 2023, Lorena was hired by that facility. She still works there and continues to pursue what she considers her life mission: “I dedicated myself to welcoming all those children that most other facilities turn away.”
D’abord en tant que mère d’enfants autis: First as the mother of autistic children, then as a childcare provider, Lorena realized that “there is an enormous lack of support for families with an ASD diagnosis.”
Elle s’ouvre également pour raconter son: She also opens up to tell her story, which helps other mothers feel less alone. Like the one who asked her whether her family knew about the diagnoses of all three of her children, because she hadn’t dared make her son’s diagnosis public. “He was a child who, at first, wanted nothing to do with daycare. Once he started spending time with me, he changed completely. He became happy to do his activities.”
L’acceptation de la famille est d’une gr: Acceptance from the family is very important, Lorena stresses. “Childhood goes by quickly, and it’s crucial to step in early, when the diagnosis has just been made.” A diagnosis that, in her view, “always stigmatizes the child,” even in a society where it will be better accepted than in Venezuela, where integrating a neurodivergent child into the regular school system is still very difficult today. When [children who have received a diagnosis] do something that falls outside what is considered ‘normal,’ people notice it much more.”
Lorena a trouvé du soutien, mais elle év: Lorena found support, but she repeatedly speaks of her “luck.” In her view, unfortunately, few parents find as many resources as she did. “There are mothers who never get to rest, who don’t have the capacity to do anything other than care for their children.”

Que pense-t-elle de son emploi actuel ?: What does she think of her current job? She answers without hesitation: “I never thought I would be this happy. I’ve become what I wanted to be. I love welcoming the children who need more attention into my group. They’re not a headache for me, they come to fill my heart.” Many of her colleagues are also immigrants, and she wants to highlight their commitment and dedication in the work they do.
Elle pense que, lorsqu’un parent reçoit: She believes that when a parent receives an autism diagnosis, they need to give themselves space. Her advice: “Cry. Live through it. Acceptance will come, but you shouldn’t rush it. It’s a grieving process and you have to go through it.”
Pour ceux qui n’ont pas encore un diagno: For those who don’t yet have a clear diagnosis but have a doubt, she advises the following: “Watch your children closely, because that suspicion will lead you to see things you hadn’t seen before.” Behind the label “ill-mannered” there can be a more complex reality, she explains. And that reality can only be revealed through a professional assessment.
Après six ans de changements, Lorena et: After six years of change, Lorena and her family are going to apply for permanent residence in Canada.
Elle souhaite continuer à suivre des étu: She wants to keep pursuing specialized studies in the education of children with disabilities, such as autism, Down syndrome or cerebral palsy. “I want to dedicate myself to helping Spanish-speaking mothers. I know it changes everything to receive care in your mother tongue. I could tell them, as a mother who has been through all this: ‘You’ll see, everything will get better.’ I think that’s where we can make a big difference,” she concludes.
